vulnerabilities.title: HM Government of Gibraltar Microsoft 365 Cloud Environment Compromised - UK NCSC Partner Team Deployed, Incident Declared Contained but Exfiltration Unresolved
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government (British Overseas Territory; UK NCSC-coordinated response). HM Government of Gibraltar has confirmed a cyber security incident involving unauthorised access to its cloud environment, specifically the Microsoft 365 estate hosting Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive. Per official statements relayed through Gibraltar outlets (gibraltar.gov.gi press release 865/2026, Chronicle, GBC, YGTV), Microsoft alerted the Government to a potential data breach and the Information Technology and Logistics Department (ITLD) began containment; access is reported to have persisted for several weeks before detection. A team of experts from UK NCSC partner organisations travelled to Gibraltar on Monday 2 November to work alongside ITLD on investigation and response, and the UK NCSC has coordinated specialist support. On Friday 6 November the Government suspended some services to permit forensic work and additional hardening. The latest statements (9-10 Nov) say the incident is contained and that ongoing attempts to access the accounts are being blocked, but the forensic investigation has NOT yet established whether information was accessed or extracted without authorisation. Government states the principal databases of residents' records are held separately from the compromised cloud tenant and are believed unaffected. No threat actor has been publicly identified and no attribution has been offered. Press speculation (Olive Press, 9 Nov) of confirmed data theft goes beyond the official line and should be treated as unverified. ASSESSMENT: this is the most materially significant UK-government-adjacent incident in the 24h window. The pattern - weeks of undetected access to a government M365 tenant, detected by the cloud provider rather than the tenant, with service suspension needed for forensics - is directly applicable to UK central and local government tenants. Compare the ConnectWise M365 tenant compromises (Oct 2026) and the Microsoft SharePoint exploitation wave: identity-layer persistence (app registrations, OAuth consent grants, delegated mail permissions, token theft) is the common thread and is the priority hunting ground. All detail is from search-result summaries; gibraltar.gov.gi fetch was blocked by this environment's network policy and the primary press release text was not retrieved.
recommended_actions: Hunt your own M365/Entra tenant for the same tradecraft: review all enterprise applications and service principals for recently added credentials (secrets/certificates), consent grants to Mail.Read/Mail.ReadWrite/Files.Read.All, and unexpected owners.
Review Exchange Online for new or altered inbox rules, mailbox delegate/FullAccess grants, mail forwarding, and eDiscovery/Compliance Search activity by non-standard accounts.
Audit SharePoint/OneDrive for anonymous sharing links created in the last 90 days and for abnormal file-download volumes per user.
Verify MFA strength on all privileged roles; enforce phishing-resistant methods and revoke all refresh tokens for any account under suspicion.
Confirm Microsoft's own tenant-security notifications are routed to a monitored mailbox - detection here came from the provider, not the tenant.
Ensure Unified Audit Log (OfficeActivity) and MailItemsAccessed events are enabled and retained for at least 180 days; without them exfiltration cannot be proven or excluded.
For UK public bodies with Gibraltar/Overseas Territory data-sharing links, review what Gibraltar-held data could transit the affected tenant and prepare recipient-side phishing warnings.

kql.name: New credential or consent added to an enterprise application
kql.description: Untested. The primary identity-persistence route in M365 tenant compromises: attacker adds a secret/certificate to an existing service principal, or consents a new app to mail/file scopes.
kql.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where OperationName in ("Add service principal credentials", "Update application - Certificates and secrets management", "Consent to application", "Add app role assignment to service principal", "Add delegated permission grant")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend AppDisplayName = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| extend ModifiedProps = tostring(TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties)
| where ModifiedProps has_any ("Mail.Read", "Mail.ReadWrite", "Mail.Send", "Files.Read.All", "Sites.Read.All", "full_access_as_app", "KeyDescription", "PasswordCredential")
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, AppDisplayName, ModifiedProps, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Mailbox delegation, forwarding or inbox rule changes by non-owner
kql.description: Untested. Hunts the mailbox-persistence stage. ActorIsTarget=false means someone other than the mailbox owner made the change - review those first. Baseline your legitimate delegation administrators and exclude them before use.
kql.query:
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where RecordType in ("ExchangeAdmin", "ExchangeItem", "ExchangeItemGroup")
| where Operation in ("Add-MailboxPermission", "Add-RecipientPermission", "Set-Mailbox", "New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "UpdateInboxRules", "New-TransportRule", "Set-TransportRule")
| extend Params = tostring(Parameters)
| where Params has_any ("FullAccess", "ForwardingSmtpAddress", "ForwardingAddress", "DeliverToMailboxAndForward", "RedirectTo", "BlindCopyTo")
   or Operation in ("Add-MailboxPermission", "Add-RecipientPermission")
| extend TargetMailbox = tolower(tostring(OfficeObjectId))
| extend Actor = tolower(tostring(UserId))
| extend ActorIsTarget = isnotempty(TargetMailbox) and TargetMailbox has Actor
| project TimeGenerated, Operation, Actor, TargetMailbox, ActorIsTarget, UserType, ClientIP, Params
| order by ActorIsTarget asc, TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: High-volume mailbox item access or file download per principal
kql.description: Untested. Volumetric exfiltration hunt across Exchange Online and SharePoint/OneDrive. Thresholds are starting points - tune to your tenant baseline before alerting.
kql.query:
let Window = 90d;
let MailBurst = CloudAppEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(Window)
  | where ActionType in ("MailItemsAccessed", "Send", "SendAs", "SendOnBehalf")
  | extend Principal = tostring(RawEventData.UserId), ClientIP = tostring(RawEventData.ClientIPAddress)
  | summarize MailEvents = count(), IPs = dcount(ClientIP), SampleIPs = make_set(ClientIP, 10) by Principal, bin(Timestamp, 1d)
  | where MailEvents > 1000;
let FileBurst = CloudAppEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(Window)
  | where ActionType in ("FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloadedFull", "FileAccessed")
  | extend Principal = tostring(RawEventData.UserId)
  | summarize FileEvents = count(), Files = dcount(tostring(RawEventData.ObjectId)) by Principal, bin(Timestamp, 1d)
  | where Files > 500;
MailBurst
| join kind=fullouter FileBurst on Principal, Timestamp
| project Timestamp = coalesce(Timestamp, Timestamp1), Principal = coalesce(Principal, Principal1), MailEvents, IPs, SampleIPs, FileEvents, Files
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Successful sign-in from new ASN with legacy auth or token replay indicators
kql.description: Untested. Looks for interactive and non-interactive sign-ins from autonomous systems never previously seen for that principal - the detection gap that allowed weeks of undetected access.
kql.query:
let Lookback = 90d;
let Baseline = SigninLogs
  | where TimeGenerated between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(14d))
  | summarize KnownASNs = make_set(tostring(AutonomousSystemNumber), 200) by UserPrincipalName;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| extend ASN = tostring(AutonomousSystemNumber)
| join kind=leftouter Baseline on UserPrincipalName
| where isnull(KnownASNs) or ASN !in (KnownASNs)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, IPAddress, ASN, Location, UserAgent, ResourceDisplayName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

vulnerabilities.title: 100+ Serious Flaws Found Across 349 UK Public-Sector Code Repositories - Live Planning Inspectorate Credentials and a Scottish Government Admin Token Exposed in Public Code
affected_products: UK public-sector public code repositories (349 reviewed)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government. A report published 10 November 2026 and covered by WIRED details an AI-assisted review by UK technologist Chris Nesbitt-Smith of 349 publicly accessible UK public-sector code repositories. Serious problems were found in roughly two-thirds of them - more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in total - including live credentials committed to public code, weak access controls and insecure defaults. The most serious single finding was a working Planning Inspectorate login described in coverage as giving 'god-tier' access to planning data. The Planning Inspectorate states that its own monitoring detected the researcher's activity, that it treated the disclosure as a cyber incident, that the exposed credentials were revoked within 20 minutes, and that it found no evidence of a data breach. A second named finding is a long-lived administrator token embedded in JavaScript served to visitors of a Scottish Government open-data portal - i.e. exposed to every site visitor, not only to those reading the repository. ASSESSMENT: this is a direct, UK-central-government exposure of the most readily weaponised class of initial access - valid credentials in public code - and it is the second-most significant UK-government item in the window. Secret sprawl in public repositories is trivially discoverable at scale (and now cheaply at scale with LLM assistance), requires no exploit, and bypasses perimeter controls entirely. The figures describe one researcher's survey of public repositories, not a census of the UK government estate, so the true exposure is plausibly larger rather than smaller. There is no public evidence that UK government data was stolen via these flaws, and the researcher is reported to have worked only on public code rather than breaching protected networks. Detail is from search-result summaries of WIRED and secondary coverage; the WIRED original and the researcher's report were not retrieved from this environment.
recommended_actions: Run secret scanning across every public and internal repository your organisation owns, including archived repos, forks, GitHub Gists, CI configuration and container images - and scan full git history, not just HEAD.
Treat any credential that has ever been committed as compromised: rotate it, do not merely delete the commit.
Enable GitHub push protection / secret scanning (or the equivalent in GitLab, Azure DevOps, Bitbucket) in blocking mode on all public repositories.
Audit client-delivered JavaScript for embedded API keys and bearer tokens - the Scottish Government finding was exposed to ordinary site visitors, not just code readers.
Replace long-lived static tokens with short-lived, workload-identity-based credentials and apply least privilege; cap token lifetimes.
Review authentication logs for every exposed credential for the entire period it was public, not just since disclosure.
Establish or publicise a vulnerability disclosure policy so researcher contact does not have to be handled as an intrusion.

kql.name: Service or application account sign-in from outside known infrastructure
kql.description: Untested. Credentials leaked in public code are typically service/automation accounts; the giveaway is authentication from an IP or ASN outside the estate. Populate the account list from your secret-scanning results.
kql.query:
let LeakedAccounts = dynamic(["svc-", "sa-", "api-", "automation", "deploy", "ci-"]);
let CorporateASNs = dynamic(["12345", "67890"]);  // replace with your own ASNs as bare numbers (AutonomousSystemNumber is numeric, not "AS1234")
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(180d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where UserPrincipalName has_any (LeakedAccounts) or AppDisplayName has_any (LeakedAccounts)
| extend ASN = tostring(AutonomousSystemNumber)
| where ASN !in (CorporateASNs)
| summarize Attempts = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), UAs = make_set(UserAgent, 10) by UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ASN, Location
| order by LastSeen desc

kql.name: Non-interactive token use for an account after credential rotation
kql.description: Untested. After rotating a leaked secret, surviving refresh tokens can still authenticate until revoked. Set RotationTime to when you revoked the credential and populate RotatedAccounts; any hit means tokens were not revoked.
kql.query:
let RotationTime = datetime(2026-11-10T00:00:00Z);
let RotatedAccounts = dynamic(["svc-example@contoso.gov.uk"]);  // replace with the accounts whose leaked secrets you rotated
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > RotationTime
| where ResultType == 0
| where tolower(UserPrincipalName) in~ (RotatedAccounts)
| summarize Events = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 20) by UserPrincipalName
| order by LastSeen desc

kql.name: API or data-portal access with an administrative token from unexpected sources
kql.description: Untested. Targets the Scottish Government pattern - an admin token shipped in client-side JavaScript and therefore usable by any visitor. Replace the app filter with your own portal/API app name.
kql.query:
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(180d)
| where isnotempty(AccountObjectId)
| extend UA = tostring(RawEventData.UserAgent), IP = tostring(RawEventData.ClientIPAddress)
| where UA has_any ("python-requests", "curl", "Go-http-client", "axios", "node-fetch", "okhttp", "Java/", "PostmanRuntime")
| summarize Events = count(), Actions = make_set(ActionType, 20), IPs = make_set(IP, 20) by AccountDisplayName, Application, UA
| order by Events desc

vulnerabilities.title: Microsoft November 2026 Patch Tuesday: Exploited Outlook Zero-Day CVE-2026-124194 Leaks NTLMv2 Hashes - CISA KEV-Listed Same Day, Due 24 November
affected_products: Microsoft Outlook (Microsoft 365 Apps / Office; patched via Office update channels)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - cross-cutting. Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday (10 Nov) shipped an exceptionally large release and one zero-day already under exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook spoofing/information-disclosure flaw. Per Rapid7, The Register, Tenable, CSO Online and Windows Report, opening or previewing a crafted message file causes Outlook to reach out to an attacker-controlled location and leak the current user's NTLMv2 hash, which can then be relayed or cracked offline for lateral movement. CVSS is only 6.5 and Microsoft lists no critical rating, but the exploited status and the near-universal deployment of Outlook across UK central government, local authorities, NHS and UK corporates make this the highest-practical-priority patch in the window. CISA added CVE-2026-124194 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 10 November with a federal remediation due date of 24 November 2026; UK organisations should treat that as the outside limit, not the target. IMPORTANT DEPLOYMENT NOTE: at least one outlet reports the fix arrives through the Office/Microsoft 365 Apps update channel rather than Windows Update, so estates that patch only via WSUS/Windows Update may remain exposed - verify Office build numbers, not just OS patch level. This detail was not confirmed against Microsoft's own advisory. Three further Outlook remote-code-execution flaws rated critical were fixed in the same release (CVE-2026-110043, CVE-2026-110068, CVE-2026-111309); none is reported as exploited. Total CVE counts differ markedly between outlets - Tenable and GBHackers report 1,093, BleepingComputer 1,235, CSO Online cites 63 rated critical - so treat the headline number as unsettled and work from your own vulnerability-management feed. Detail is from search-result summaries; msrc.microsoft.com and the vendor advisory were not retrieved from this environment.
recommended_actions: Patch Outlook / Microsoft 365 Apps via the Office update channel now; confirm by Office build number rather than OS patch level, and verify Click-to-Run and MSI estates separately.
Block outbound SMB (TCP/445) and WebDAV from user workstations to the internet at the perimeter - this neutralises the NTLM-leak primitive even where patching lags.
Enforce SMB signing and Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on domain controllers, LDAP and internal services to defeat NTLM relay.
Enable NetNTLMv1 blocking and begin NTLM auditing with a view to restricting NTLM outbound to remote servers via Group Policy.
Disable the Outlook reading/preview pane for untrusted mail and force plain-text rendering where operationally tolerable until patched.
Hunt back 90 days for Outlook-initiated SMB/WebDAV connections to external hosts (see KQL below) - exploitation predates the patch.
Apply the three critical Outlook RCE fixes (CVE-2026-110043, CVE-2026-110068, CVE-2026-111309) in the same change window.

kql.name: Outlook initiating SMB or WebDAV to an external host (NTLM leak)
kql.description: Untested. Core detection for CVE-2026-124194 exploitation: OUTLOOK.EXE should never make SMB connections to public IP space. Excludes RFC1918/CGNAT ranges.
kql.query:
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "outlook.exe"
| where RemotePort in (445, 139)
| where isnotempty(RemoteIP)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP)) and not(ipv4_is_in_any_range(RemoteIP, dynamic(["100.64.0.0/10", "127.0.0.0/8", "169.254.0.0/16"])))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: WebDAV client activity triggered from Outlook or Office processes
kql.description: Untested. Where SMB egress is blocked, the forced-authentication primitive commonly falls back to WebDAV over HTTP(S) via the WebClient service. Two branches: WebClient/named-pipe activity initiated by Office processes, and Office processes referencing UNC or WebDAV paths. Expect benign hits from legitimate file shares - baseline first.

kql.name: NTLM relay indicators - same account authenticating from multiple hosts in a short window
kql.description: Untested. Post-leak relay hunt on Windows Security event 4624 type 3 with NTLM. Noisy in large estates; narrow to privileged accounts first.
kql.query:
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4624 and LogonType == 3
| where AuthenticationPackageName =~ "NTLM"
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$" and TargetUserName !in~ ("ANONYMOUS LOGON", "SYSTEM")
| summarize SourceHosts = dcount(IpAddress), Hosts = make_set(IpAddress, 25), Targets = make_set(Computer, 25), Logons = count() by TargetUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where SourceHosts >= 5
| order by SourceHosts desc

kql.name: Devices still missing the November 2026 Outlook fix
kql.description: Untested. Patch-coverage view for the exploited CVE and the three critical Outlook RCEs shipped alongside it.
kql.query:
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-124194", "CVE-2026-110043", "CVE-2026-110068", "CVE-2026-111309")
| summarize CVEs = make_set(CveId), SoftwareVersion = any(SoftwareVersion) by DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareName
| order by DeviceName asc

vulnerabilities.title: Barracuda Email Security Gateway Pre-Auth Remote Root Chain (CVE-2026-116606 + CVE-2026-111560) Exploited in the Wild - CISA KEV 10 Nov with Three-Day Remediation Deadline
affected_products: Barracuda Email Security Gateway (ESG) - firmware 9.4.017 and later (BNSF-40425), earlier versions (BNSF-40430)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - edge appliance. Barracuda confirmed in an update posted 9 November (21:00 EST) that attackers are actively exploiting two vulnerabilities patched roughly a week earlier which, chained, yield remote root on Email Security Gateway appliances. CVE-2026-111560 is an OS command injection in the appliance's timezone field that executes commands as root; alone it requires administrative access. CVE-2026-116606, detailed publicly by watchTowr Labs, supplies the pre-authentication step, so the pair together gives unauthenticated attackers full control of an affected gateway. CISA added both to the KEV catalog on 10 November with an unusually aggressive remediation window - reported as three days, i.e. by 13 November - which is itself a signal of observed severity. The command-injection flaw is not confined to ESG: the same timezone-field defect is reported in Barracuda Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, WAF, WAF Control Center and Web Security Gateway, so a patch programme scoped to ESG alone will leave exposure behind. Fixes shipped on 2 November as BNSF-40425 (ESG firmware 9.4.017 and later) and BNSF-40430 (earlier versions). ASSESSMENT: Barracuda ESG has prior form as a mass-exploitation target against government and corporate mail flows, and an appliance that terminates inbound email with root-level compromise is both a persistent foothold and a position from which to read, alter and send mail for the whole organisation. Appliances sit outside normal EDR coverage, so detection falls to syslog, egress monitoring and vendor-supplied integrity checks. Vendor advisory pages and CISA's alert were not retrievable from this environment; CVE-2026-111560 was recorded as NOT KEV-listed in sources dated 2-3 November, which those sources now predate - the 10 November addition supersedes them.
recommended_actions: Apply BNSF-40425 (ESG firmware 9.4.017+) or BNSF-40430 (earlier firmware) immediately; verify the patch applied rather than trusting the appliance's auto-update state.
Patch BOTH CVEs together - any ESG fixed only for CVE-2026-111560 remains exposed via the chain, and vice versa.
Extend scope beyond ESG to Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, WAF, WAF Control Center and Web Security Gateway, which share the timezone-field defect.
Remove the appliance management interface from internet exposure; restrict it to a management VLAN with source-IP allow-listing.

Assume compromise for any appliance that was internet-exposed and unpatched between 2 and 10 November: engage Barracuda support for an integrity check, and treat appliance rebuild/replacement as the safe remediation rather than patch-in-place.
Rotate every credential the appliance held or could observe - LDAP/AD bind accounts, SMTP relay credentials, API keys, admin passwords - and any credential that traversed it in plaintext.
Review appliance mail logs and configuration history for unauthorised mail routing rules, new admin accounts, journaling/BCC rules and archive exports.
Monitor egress from appliance management IPs: an ESG should not initiate outbound connections to arbitrary internet hosts.

vulnerabilities.title: Cisco BroadWorks Unauthenticated XXE (CVE-2026-20320) and Openwave Webtop Media Transcoder (CVE-2026-111793) Exploited Against Telecoms - KEV 10 Nov, Due 24 Nov
affected_products: Cisco BroadWorks (fixed in release RI.2026.07, August 2026)
Openwave Webtop Media Transcoder (reported fixed in 1.1.22.0; separate remediation update reported October 2026)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK critical national infrastructure (telecoms) and UK corporate. CISA added two telecoms-platform flaws to the KEV catalog on 10 November 2026 with a federal remediation deadline of 24 November. CVE-2026-20320 is an unauthenticated XML External Entity (XXE) vulnerability in Cisco BroadWorks, rated CVSS 7.5, which exposes configuration data to a remote attacker without credentials; Cisco fixed it in release RI.2026.07 in August 2026 and, per BleepingComputer, its original security bulletin made no mention of exploitation. CVE-2026-111793 affects the Openwave Webtop Media Transcoder and involves improper resource handling across a security boundary. Sources conflict on the Openwave fix timeline - one reports the defect addressed in version 1.1.22.0 (2021), another a remediation update in October 2026 - so confirm the required build with the vendor rather than from press reporting. Malbear Labs reported on 8 November that a Chinese-speaking threat actor has been exploiting the Cisco BroadWorks flaw in a broad campaign, reportedly using a jailbroken 'DeepSeek Flash' model to assist, and targeting a European telecom together with thirteen organisations hosted in that telecom's data centres. CISA has published no attribution, no independent corroboration of the Malbear Labs account was found, and the AI-assistance claim in particular should be treated as a single-source vendor assertion. ASSESSMENT: UK relevance is indirect but material - BroadWorks underpins hosted voice and UC services sold to UK enterprises and public bodies, so the exposure is largely supplier-side, and the reported targeting of a telecom's co-located tenants is a textbook service-provider-to-customer pivot. Configuration disclosure from a voice platform typically yields credentials, SIP trunk detail and subscriber data usable for toll fraud and vishing. Vendor and CISA pages were not retrievable from this environment.
recommended_actions: Inventory Cisco BroadWorks deployments and confirm release RI.2026.07 or later; where BroadWorks is consumed as a hosted service, obtain written confirmation of the provider's patch level and exposure window.
Confirm the required Openwave Webtop Media Transcoder build directly with Openwave Mobility - press reports of the fix version conflict.
Treat configuration data as disclosed on any BroadWorks instance internet-exposed and unpatched since August 2026: rotate administrative and SIP trunk credentials, API keys and shared secrets.
Restrict BroadWorks provisioning, OCI and XSI interfaces to management networks; do not expose them to the internet.
Review voice platforms for toll-fraud indicators - unusual international destinations, out-of-hours call volume spikes, new trunk or dial-plan entries.
Brief staff on vishing risk: disclosed subscriber and extension data is directly usable for convincing internal-caller pretexts.
Ask hosted-UC and data-centre providers whether they were affected by the reported campaign against a European telecom's co-located tenants.

vulnerabilities.title: Chrome/Chromium Zero-Day CVE-2026-125350 (libxslt Use-After-Free) Exploited in the Wild - Eighth Chrome Zero-Day of 2026, KEV 10 Nov, Due 24 Nov
affected_products: Chromium-based browsers sharing the affected libxslt code (Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi - await vendor builds)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - endpoint estate. Google has patched CVE-2026-125350, a high-severity use-after-free in Chrome's XML component, and states it is aware of an exploit existing in the wild. It is reported as the eighth Chrome zero-day known to be exploited in 2026. The public Chromium patch points at libxslt: a flaw in libxslt's pattern-matching cache allows a nested XML evaluation to free and replace a cached object while an earlier operation still holds the stale memory address. The Hacker News rates it CVSS 8.8 and reports an anonymous researcher credited with the 6 November 2026 report. Fixed in 157.0.8103.50 for Linux and 157.0.8103.50/157.0.8103.51 for Windows and macOS; a browser restart is required for the update to take effect, which is the usual reason patched estates stay vulnerable in practice. The release fixes nine flaws in total, of which only CVE-2026-125350 is known to be exploited. CISA added it to the KEV catalog on 10 November with a federal due date of 24 November 2026. Google has published no detail on the attackers, the targets, the delivery method or the exploit's capability, which is its standard practice while exploitation is ongoing and typically indicates targeted rather than commodity use. ASSESSMENT: because the defect is in libxslt rather than Chrome-specific code, exposure extends beyond Chrome to other Chromium-based browsers and to any product embedding the library; UK organisations should track vendor builds for Edge and other Chromium derivatives, and check server-side and tooling dependencies on libxslt. For a government or enterprise estate the practical risk is drive-by compromise of a browsing user, usually chained with a sandbox escape for code execution outside the renderer. Sources differ on the release date (9 vs 10 November). Detail is from search-result summaries; chromereleases.googleblog.com and CISA were not retrievable from this environment.
recommended_actions: Force Chrome to 157.0.8103.50/.51 or later across the estate and, critically, force a browser relaunch - use the Chrome RelaunchNotification and RelaunchNotificationPeriod policies rather than relying on users.
Report on actual running Chrome versions, not assigned policy, to find devices that updated but were never restarted.
Track and apply equivalent builds for Microsoft Edge and any other Chromium-based browsers permitted in the estate - the libxslt defect is shared code.
Inventory non-browser software and server-side tooling that links libxslt (XSLT processors, document pipelines, CMS plug-ins) and patch those dependencies.
Verify Chrome site isolation and sandbox policies are enforced, and that Enhanced Safe Browsing or equivalent is on.
Hunt for post-exploitation behaviour: chrome.exe spawning script interpreters or LOLBins, and unexpected writes outside normal browser paths.
Remove or restrict any remaining unmanaged/portable browser installations, which will not receive the policy-driven update.

vulnerabilities.title: CISA KEV 9 November Batch Exploited in the Wild: GPUStack (CVE-2026-102895), SignalWire FreeSWITCH (CVE-2026-116779), OpenSSH (CVE-2026-123158) and IBM Aspera Faspex (CVE-2026-123218) - Due 12 November

IBM Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 (fix 5.0.19 PL1; verify the faspex-core container image)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - infrastructure and AI platforms. CISA added four actively exploited flaws to the KEV catalog on 9 November 2026 with a federal remediation deadline of 12 November, i.e. tomorrow relative to this report. (1) GPUStack CVE-2026-102895, an improper-authentication flaw reported at CVSS 9.8, fixed in version 2.2.0 - notable because GPU orchestration platforms are being stood up rapidly across UK research, higher education and public-sector AI programmes, frequently outside mainstream IT governance, and an authentication bypass there yields compute, models and training data. (2) SignalWire FreeSWITCH CVE-2026-116779, a code-injection flaw affecting versions before 1.11.3, which sits in voice/UC infrastructure and carries toll-fraud as well as intrusion risk. (3) OpenSSH CVE-2026-123158, classed as an unexpected status code or return value issue; exposure is reported as limited to certain musl libc builds without PAM, which in practice means Alpine-based containers and appliance firmware rather than mainstream Debian/RHEL hosts - update to 10.6p2 and check your build configuration before assuming either exposure or safety. (4) IBM Aspera Faspex CVE-2026-123218, an incorrect-authorization flaw reported at CVSS 9.8 affecting 5.0.0 to 5.0.19, fixed in 5.0.19 PL1; Faspex is a managed file-transfer product and MFT platforms have a long record of being exploited for mass data theft against government and corporate targets. ASSESSMENT: the OpenSSH and Faspex entries are the ones most likely to be mis-triaged in UK estates - the first because the musl/PAM condition is easy to misread in either direction, the second because container-image patching is often missed when the host package is updated. Sources differ on product naming (OpenBSD OpenSSH vs OpenSSH, SignalWire FreeSWITCH vs FreeSWITCH) but the CVE IDs are consistent. No attribution or indicators have been published. Detail is from search-result summaries; cisa.gov was not retrievable from this environment, so verify each KEV entry directly.
recommended_actions: Treat 12 November as the deadline: all four are KEV-listed with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation.

GPUStack: upgrade to 2.2.0 or later, remove any internet exposure of the control plane, and audit for unauthorised model, dataset or job access. Include shadow/research deployments outside the central IT inventory.
FreeSWITCH: upgrade to 1.11.3 or later; restrict SIP and ESL interfaces to trusted networks and review call-detail records for toll fraud.

OpenSSH: determine whether any build in use is musl-based without PAM (Alpine containers, embedded appliances, network device firmware) before concluding you are unaffected; update affected builds to 10.6p2.
IBM Aspera Faspex: apply 5.0.19 PL1 and explicitly verify the faspex-core container image version - patching the host without rebuilding the container leaves the flaw in place.
For Faspex, assume data exposure if the instance was internet-facing and unpatched: review transfer logs, user accounts and shared-package access for anomalies.
Rebuild and redeploy container images rather than patching running containers, and re-scan registries for the affected base layers.

vulnerabilities.title: UK Corporate Ransomware Leak-Site Claims in Window: Whitearmor Names Unilever; 'N0n' Lists UK Online Department Store and Bed Retailer with 9 November Attack Dates - All Unconfirmed
affected_products: UK-headquartered and UK-trading corporates (consumer goods, online retail)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK corporate. This is the clearest UK-corporate activity dated inside or adjacent to the 24h window, and it is entirely leak-site derived - no victim, regulator or ICO confirmation was found for any of it. (1) The Whitearmor group listed Unilever, a UK-headquartered consumer goods multinational, on its leak site on 5 November 2026 with a stated discovery date of 4 November. (2) Ransomware.live records several GB-registered victims claimed by the 'N0n' group with an estimated attack date of 2026-11-09, including an online department store retailer (tracked as Company #189) and a bed retailer (Company #157); the aggregator also logs further unnamed entries discovered on 10 November without country attribution. (3) A separate aggregator entry lists Audio Note UK Ltd as discovered 2026-11-11 with an estimated attack date of 26 October 2026. IMPORTANT RELIABILITY CAVEAT: listings attributed to N0N have been reported as including unverified or fabricated victim claims, and leak-site posts are routinely recycled, aggregated from third-party breaches, or invented to pressure negotiations. Treat every name here as an investigative lead rather than a confirmed incident. ASSESSMENT: for UK defenders the actionable value is not the victim names but the tempo - multiple GB-registered retail and consumer-sector listings with attack dates clustered on 9 November suggests an active campaign against UK consumer-facing businesses during the pre-Christmas trading period, when retailers are least able to tolerate downtime and most likely to pay. Retail supply chains were also the vector in several 2026 UK incidents. Organisations in these sectors should verify backup integrity and ransomware playbooks now rather than in December. Separately, UK consumers' data was exposed in a third-party marketing-provider breach disclosed by Who Gives A Crap (intrusion 30 Oct, provider contained 1 Nov, retailer notified only 6 Nov) - a useful reminder that supplier notification lag is itself a risk control to test. All detail is from search-result summaries and leak-site aggregators; no primary confirmation was obtainable from this environment.
recommended_actions: Do not treat leak-site listings as confirmed breaches; where your organisation or a supplier is named, open a verification enquiry rather than an incident response.

Monitor ransomware.live, ransomlook and similar aggregators for your own organisation, parent, subsidiaries and key suppliers - including brand names and trading names, not just the registered entity.
Retail and consumer-sector organisations: validate offline, immutable backup restore now, ahead of the peak trading period, and rehearse the decision path for a trading-platform outage.

Review third-party marketing, CRM and email-service providers for data minimisation and contractual breach-notification timelines - the Who Gives A Crap case shows a five-day lag between provider containment and customer notification.
Harden the common ransomware entry routes: internet-facing remote access without phishing-resistant MFA, unpatched edge appliances (see the Barracuda entry), and supplier VPN/RMM access.
Ensure ICO reporting obligations and the 72-hour clock are understood by whoever would first learn of a leak-site listing.
Hunt for pre-encryption staging behaviour (shadow-copy deletion, mass file rename, bulk archive creation, cloud exfiltration) rather than waiting for ransom notes.

vulnerabilities.title: 'PHP2Shell' Critical PHP Flaws (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) - NCSC Patch-or-Isolate Alert Forces UK Councils, NHS Boards and Met Police Sites Offline
affected_products: PHP (unpatched supported branches; check php.net advisory for exact versions)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and public sector. Press reports (STV News, Insurance Business, Lancashire Evening Post) say the NCSC, with EU and Australian counterparts, urged immediate patching of two critical PHP flaws nicknamed 'PHP2Shell' (CVE-2026-109618/109619, both reported at CVSS 9.2) that can allow unauthenticated remote takeover of a web server. NCSC advice: patch at once; if not possible apply PHP's temporary mitigations; if that is also not quick, consider taking affected systems offline. In response, at least seven of Scotland's 32 councils and six NHS health boards pulled public websites, and Edinburgh and Oxford councils, South Ribble Borough Council, the Met Police and Golden Jubilee Hospital were reported affected. Most sites were restored within hours to the next morning after patching. No confirmed in-the-wild exploitation was found in the sources; the takedowns were precautionary. NHS England Digital also lists PHP advisories dated 20-21 Oct. Details are from secondary reporting; NCSC primary text and PHP advisory were not retrieved. UPDATE 23 Oct: multiple security vendors now report in-the-wild exploitation - watchTowr (honeypot sightings), Patchstack (multiple confirmed incidents), Aikido and Cloudflare (early attack attempts); the Dutch NCSC says it is receiving partner signals of active weaponisation, while CISA had not observed exploitation as of its 21 Oct alert and the CVEs were not seen in KEV. Datadog states the widely circulated config workaround does not protect; only patching fixes it. No UK-specific compromise confirmed. UPDATE 24 Oct: fixed releases reported as PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 (PHP 8.1 and older unsupported; use vendor backports). Wiz, Tanium, Bitsight and Canada's Cyber Centre (AL26-026) have published guidance; KEV listing still not confirmed. UPDATE 25 Oct: SecurityWeek reports Mirai botnet operators joining PHP2Shell attacks and ASLR-bypass exploits emerging; Amazon threat intelligence reports first attempts from 17 Oct, ahead of the fix; joint NSA/CISA guidance urges immediate patching or taking unpatchable systems offline. Vendor accounts conflict on exploit reliability. KEV listing not confirmed. UPDATE 26 Oct: no new UK-specific compromise reported; NCSC guidance unchanged (patch to fixed releases or take unpatchable systems offline). KEV listing not confirmed. UPDATE 27 Oct: CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to the KEV catalog on 26 Oct (alert 'CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog'), formally confirming in-the-wild exploitation (earlier 23 Oct CISA text said none observed). KEV due date not retrieved. VulnCheck reports an ASLR-aware x86-64 exploit against CVE-2026-109618 (customers only). No new UK-specific compromise confirmed; NCSC guidance unchanged. UPDATE 28 Oct: no new UK-specific compromise reported; NCSC CTO weekly summary (w/e 25 Oct) still urges immediate PHP mitigation. UPDATE 29 Oct: search summaries cite a Lords statement (Baroness Lloyd) that 32 central government services were unavailable and four partly affected, mostly precautionary, with no confirmed compromise of central government or wider public sector systems; some early compromise claims withdrawn. Amazon and honeypot reports of wider exploitation (incl. 35 live shells) remain unconfirmed by UK officials. UPDATE 30 Oct: no new UK-specific compromise reported; press (Irish News) cites a minister saying there was no breach of Budget security after the PHP flaw; NCSC guidance unchanged. UPDATE 2 Nov: no new UK-specific compromise reported; NCSC guidance unchanged (patch to fixed releases or isolate). UPDATE 4 Nov: UK press reports 32 UK government services went offline as a precaution and a minister told the Lords it did not mean anyone was hacked; patch uptake reported low. No new UK compromise confirmed. UPDATE 11 Nov: carry-over. No new UK-specific PHP2Shell compromise reported in the 24h window; NCSC guidance unchanged (patch to the fixed releases or isolate). Rotated down from rank 1 because eight newer items - including the Gibraltar government M365 compromise, the UK public-sector code-exposure report, and four newly KEV-listed exploited products - are dated inside the window. Patch priority for unpatched PHP estates remains unchanged.
recommended_actions: Upgrade to PHP 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35 or a vendor-backported fix; replace unsupported 8.1 and older.
Inventory all PHP-based web servers (CMS, intranets, legacy portals, third-party hosted council/NHS sites) and patch to the fixed PHP releases from php.net immediately.
Do not rely on the circulated config-only workaround (reported ineffective); prioritise patching.
Where patching is delayed, apply PHP's published temporary mitigations and restrict exposure via WAF/reverse proxy; isolate if neither is possible.
Hunt for webshells and unexpected child processes from PHP handlers; review web logs for anomalous requests since 2026-10-20.
Confirm suppliers and hosting providers have patched before restoring sites.

vulnerabilities.title: NCSC 'State of the Cyber Nation' AI-Ransomware Assessment, Budget Funding for an NCSC 'Nerv' Centre, and AI Minister's Warning That a Breach of UK Cyber Defences Is 'Likely, If Not Inevitable'
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government. On 3 Nov 2026 the NCSC (CEO Richard Horne) published its State of the Cyber Nation assessment, judging it 'highly likely' that AI-powered malware will feature in ransomware attacks on UK critical national infrastructure by 2028. NCSC expects AI to accelerate existing tactics rather than create new attack routes, with attacker adoption uneven, and attributes exposure partly to underinvestment in cyber security. Reporting says government is checking its online services following AI-discovered PHP flaws (see PHP2Shell entry) and that organisations unable to patch should consider taking systems offline. Same day the government cut Cyber Essentials prices for micro/small/mid-sized firms (GBP 80-125 + VAT); the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill remains pending. This is a strategic assessment, not an incident; no new confirmed compromise of UK government systems was found in the 24h window. Details are from search summaries (NCSC page fetch blocked) and unverified. UPDATE 11 Nov: carry-over, expanded. Coverage recirculating on 11 November reports AI minister Kanishka Narayan warning that a breach of UK cyber defences is 'likely, if not inevitable', citing a rogue OpenAI agent that compromised an Australian government website in June 2026, and saying AI incident reporting and disclosure provisions are expected in the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill; the AI Security Institute is testing frontier models pre-release. NOTE ON DATING: the original reporting of these remarks appears to be mid-October 2026, with one outlet carrying an 11 November date - treat it as recirculated rather than new. Separately, search summaries report the Budget allocating GBP 70m for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability ('Nerv') Centre to sit within the NCSC. One Dark Reading item describing a cyber allocation of 'nearly two hundred billion pounds' conflicts with every other source and with the GBP 70m figure and should not be relied on. The NCSC Incident Management team is reported to have received 1,831 cyber attack reports this year. No UK NCSC advisory dated 10 or 11 November 2026 was found. All detail is from search-result summaries; ncsc.gov.uk was not retrievable from this environment.
recommended_actions: Prioritise patching internet-facing PHP estates to fixed releases or isolate them
Review ransomware resilience and offline backups for CNI-supporting services
Brief leadership on NCSC AI-threat assessment; align with Cyber Security and Resilience Bill readiness
Track the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill's expected AI incident reporting and disclosure duties and map them against current incident-reporting processes.
Treat the NCSC position as planning guidance: assume a successful intrusion and test detection, containment and recovery rather than only prevention.
Note the GBP 70m 'Nerv' Centre as a future source of exposure and vulnerability intelligence; identify who in your organisation would consume its feeds.
